extracted.intended_audience: scholars and journals considering or organizing adversarial collaborations (particularly behavioral and social scientists), potential arbiters, and early-career researchers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for planning, conducting, and judging adversarial collaborations (ACs) — structured collaborations between investigators with clashing models — including recommendations on team selection, procedures, documentation, arbitration, and analytic strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose your adversary wisely
rubrics_metrics.description: Select collaborators/adversaries who share a commitment to truth and have suitable interpersonal qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective adversaries are described as having “a common commitment to the truth and a willingness to not just engage genuinely with the collaboration, but to learn from their adversaries.” Recommended traits: respect for others' work, intellectual humility, openness, calmness, friendliness, generosity. Avoid individuals lacking temperament for ACs. (Table 4 recommendations and participant quotes.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Be a good adversary yourself
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants must manage their own behavior to foster a respectful, open, and constructive collaborative culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice includes: “Check your ego at the door and remember that you're a scientist,” “Hold your beliefs lightly,” practice social intelligence, flexibility, humor, and respect. Focus on your own conduct rather than anticipating opponent misbehavior. (Table 4 quotes and discussion under 'For success'.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Involve a neutral arbiter
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a third-party mediator trusted by both sides to settle design disputes, manage conflict, and maintain fairness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arbiters should be “trusted and respected by both parties” and capable of keeping calm and negotiating compromises. Their roles include mitigating conflict (pausing meetings, splitting email threads), making impartial analytic decisions (e.g., blinding to conditions), and pushing collaborators to maintain momentum and meet deadlines. (Sections: 'Be a neutral arbiter', 'Additional insights from Arbiters'.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep extensive documentation including pre-project agreements
rubrics_metrics.description: Document beliefs, predictions, conditional beliefs, agreements, methods, and decisions thoroughly before and during the project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Participants urged to be “meticulous about notes, predictions, beliefs, conditional beliefs and write everything down!” Pre-project agreements can function “almost as a contract” to hold collaborators accountable. Detailed transparent documentation aligns with open science practices and helps resolve disputes. (Table 4 and multiple recommendations.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-register methodology and ensure data openness
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-register study methods and analytic plans and commit to open sharing of data and materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article stresses “Precise pre-registrations [and] data openness” and that “the methodology must be well pre-registered beforehand.” Pre-registration reduces post-hoc disputes about analytic choices; data openness supports transparency and replication. Combining ACs with Registered Reports (RRs) is recommended to protect against publication bias and peer-review incentives for flashy claims. (Discussion and Table 4.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Agree up front on operationalizations, methods, and what counts as success
rubrics_metrics.description: Collaborators should negotiate and document construct operationalizations, measurement choices, and criteria for success before data collection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Participants emphasized that “we had to all agree up front what a good project looked like” to avoid later arguments about selectively chosen data or analyses. Resolving differences in operationalization early is critical since methodological choices drive divergent results; clear, agreed-upon protocols aid fairness and interpretability. (Multiple sections, e.g., 'ACs are more challenging...' and Table 2/4.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Designate individuals to ensure steady progress and provide incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign persons (often junior co-authors or an arbiter) responsibility for maintaining momentum and coordinating tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper notes: “The determination and effort of the most junior co-authors helped immensely.” An arbiter may need to motivate collaborators when stalled. Having incentives and multiple people at various career stages helps distribute workload and keeps the project moving. (Table 4 and 'Additional insights from Arbiters'.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Involve early career scholars strategically
rubrics_metrics.description: Include junior researchers who may be less committed to prior theories and can perform much of the legwork and analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Participants recommended integrating junior researchers because they are often more open-minded, contribute effort that maintains momentum, and can help reconcile perspectives (e.g., one junior colleague spending time in the other's lab). This can mitigate vested-interest effects among senior scholars. (Table 4 quotes.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use rigorous analytic strategies (multiverse approaches, pretesting) to expose robustness and boundary conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ multiple analyses, pretesting, and robustness checks to reveal how results depend on choices and contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arbiters praised pretesting and the “multiverse approach,” which enabled multiple analyses across contexts and helped show that both sides could be partially right in different circumstances. Such strategies reduce the likelihood of declaring a single 'winner' and increase the nuance and generalizability of findings. (Sections on arbiters and discussion.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Select questions appropriate for ACs and manage expectations about outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Use ACs when a genuine, well-defined disagreement exists and when participants are willing to accept nuanced outcomes rather than expecting a definitive winner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cautions ACs are not suited to every topic or scholar: they work best when investigators have the temperament and there is a clear disagreement. Participants should expect ACs to be more challenging, produce more nuanced findings, and often result in deeper understanding rather than wholesale belief reversal. Plan accordingly. (Discussion: 'works best when investigators possess the right temperament' and 'ACs produce more nuanced findings'.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider registered reports and journal structures to protect scientific incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Pair ACs with Registered Reports or advocate for journal processes that reward rigor over sensational findings to reduce publication bias against nuanced AC results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors recommend conducting ACs alongside Registered Reports (RRs), arguing journals that accept methods before data collection can better publish the subtle, rigorous outcomes typical of ACs. They also suggest journals or conferences could organize ACs to systematize and scale the approach. (Discussion and Conclusion.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Foster a shared commitment to careful operationalization, rigorous methodology, and circumspect interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasize fair construct operationalization, rigorous methods, and cautious verbal claims to improve study validity and generalizability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ACs are touted as a remedy for methodological and conceptual shortcomings by embedding diverse perspectives throughout design, analysis, and interpretation. The goal is to produce 'fair construct operationalization, rigorous methodology, and circumspect verbal descriptions of findings' so results avoid overstated generalizations and better map boundary conditions. (Introduction and multiple sections.)
